description: CrewCheck: crew health when Earth is far away. Near Earth, a flight surgeon answers in seconds; on the way to Mars, a reply takes up to 20 minutes each way. CrewCheck collects vitals automatically from a wearable, needs under a minute of input a day, and shows each crew member on a living body map. For every signal it says who acts: the astronaut, the crew medical officer, or Earth. AI advises, rules decide. We have built personal health software before. Teammates welcome.
summary: CrewCheck is a health panel for a deep-space crew where rules with NASA sources decide, on board, who acts, and the answer depends on how far Earth is. Switch the mission from the ISS to a Mars transit and the same signals change hands: near Earth the flight surgeon answers in seconds; with a reply up to 20 minutes one way, the astronaut or the crew medical officer acts first. Every verdict comes from visible rules with thresholds and sources, measured against each astronaut's personal norm rather than a population average. Weak signals that drift together (sleep, mood, blood pressure) are read as one pattern before any single value crosses a line. An AI advisor only explains; an onboard agent runs the case within explicit limits and follows it to a re-measure and an honest result, such as "Partly worked". Vitals come in automatically from a suit (simulated, modelled on the CSA Bio-Monitor); the crew spends under a minute a day on input, for one person or the whole crew. Synthetic data only; not a medical device.
details:
THE IDEA IN ONE LINE. On board, rules with NASA sources decide who acts, the astronaut, the crew medic or Earth, depending on how long Earth takes to answer; AI only explains.

1. DISTANCE CHANGES WHO DECIDES. Switch ISS, Moon, Mars transit or Mars surface, or press Compare (Near Earth / Deep space). The body is the same, the signals are the same, the verdict moves: "Ask the flight surgeon, reply in seconds" near Earth, "Handle it yourself, report sent to Earth" far away. On the Moon Earth answers in seconds but home is about three days away, so the crew medic decides together with the flight surgeon. The communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way comes from NASA HRP (Distance from Earth).

2. TRANSPARENT RULES. 30 rules (29 thresholds and one linked-signal pattern) decide status and escalation; only this layer can change a verdict. The verdict reads "Decided by rules" and shows a mini-scale: the personal norm, the threshold and today's value. The Sources screen lists every rule with its threshold source (or a "Demo assumption" label) and a "Why in space" link to the NASA HRP page behind it.

3. AI EXPLAINS, THE AGENT HAS LIMITS. An AI advisor (Claude) writes a note for the crew medic and answers three fixed questions. It receives only structured data, never free text, and cannot change a status (enforced by a test). The onboard agent moves each case through Watch, Flag, Plan, Act, Verify. It may watch, notify Earth, schedule a re-measure, draft a report, page the medic and track the case; it never diagnoses, chooses medicines, closes a red case alone or changes a threshold. What the agent can do on its own grows with distance from Earth (a design assumption, stated on the Sources screen). Every clinical step waits for a person to press Approve.

4. PERSONAL NORM, NOT A POPULATION AVERAGE. Drift rules compare each astronaut with their own first two weeks in flight, so a rise of 12 mmHg above a person's own norm is flagged even inside the general normal range.

5. WEAK SIGNALS AS ONE PATTERN. Sleep, mood and blood pressure that are each only slightly off are read together and raise the tier earlier than each would alone.

6. A CASE IS FOLLOWED TO THE END. After the action CrewCheck re-measures and reports honestly: worked, "Partly worked" or not yet.

HOW TO SEE IT. Press Play story for a short guided case on a Mars transit, run on the real app state, then try it yourself: drag the mission day, switch distance, tap a body zone to see why. A forecast reads the last 21 days and warns how many days remain before a threshold. Every recommendation carries a badge: Proven, Hypothesis or Ask medic. My day shows the astronaut what the rules ask of them today, with day rings; clinical steps stay with the crew medic. The crew monitor shows four members and the cabin environment: when several crew members show the same symptom at once and a cabin reading such as CO2 is off, it flags a likely shared cause, "Cabin cause, not crew" (a hypothesis).

NASA DATA AND METHOD. The challenge has no official dataset of astronaut health indicators. CrewCheck is built on the NASA Human Research Program resources from the challenge Resources tab, which the organizers confirmed meet the NASA data requirement: the five hazards set the structure of the body map; the risk pages set which indicators we ask for and which countermeasures we suggest; the communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way, from the Distance from Earth page, drives the whole "who acts" logic. On the Sources screen each of the 30 rules shows its threshold source and a "Why in space" link to the NASA HRP page behind it. The crew data is synthetic, generated openly with a fixed seed and documented in a data passport.

NASA HAZARDS TO INDICATORS. The body map follows NASA HRP's five hazards: radiation (estimated dose by mission), isolation and confinement (sleep, mood), distance from Earth (escalation and reply time), gravity fields (exercise, body mass, vision and headache for SANS, blood pressure, heart rate), hostile closed environment (temperature, symptoms).

BENEFITS. Crews far from Earth get a first responder that notices early, explains why and shows who acts. The same logic fits Antarctic stations, ships and remote clinics on Earth.

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS SIMULATED. Real: the rules, thresholds and their sources, the forecast, the agent's limits, the live AI advisor. Simulated: four fictional crew members over 180 days from an open generator with a fixed seed and a data passport, the suit stream, the downlink to Earth. No real astronaut data. Not a medical device.

NEXT. Validate thresholds and escalation with flight surgeons; connect a real wearable; run the advisor on board.

TOOLS. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step, hand-written SVG, Chart.js, service worker for offline use, Node test suite (91 tests), GitHub Pages. Small Node proxy for the live advisor. Licence Apache 2.0. Code: https://github.com/PaulBurgEth/crewcheck
dataRefs: NASA HRP: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight (body map frame, hazard texts)
NASA HRP: Hazard Distance from Earth (up to 20 min one way, escalation logic)
NASA HRP: Hazard Gravity Fields (bone loss 1-1.5% a month, fluid shift)
NASA HRP: Risks of Human Spaceflight (SANS, fitness, sleep)
NASA HRP: Hazard Isolation and Confinement
NASA HRP: Hazard Hostile and Closed Environments
NASA HRP: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
NASA HRP: Risk of Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders
NASA HRP: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses
NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 Rev C, Crew Health
projectRefs: CSA Bio-Monitor: data model of the simulated suit stream (modelled on, not integrated with)
CSA: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
SwRI on MSL RAD: about 1.8 mSv a day in cruise (demo estimate)
ADA: low blood glucose below 70 mg/dL
CDC: adults need 7 or more hours of sleep
Anthropic API (Claude): AI advisor in the product; Claude Code for development
CrewCheck source code, synthetic data generator and data passport (Apache 2.0)
Health Canada: residential indoor air guideline for CO2 (Earth reference, not a spacecraft norm)
NIOSH: occupational noise limit 85 dBA (Earth reference, not a spacecraft norm)
OSHA: office temperature and humidity guidance (Earth reference, not a spacecraft norm)
OSHA 1926.56: office lighting (Earth reference, not a spacecraft norm)
